clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant syndrome caused by germline CDC73 (formerly HRPT2) variants affecting parafibromin.
Primary hyperparathyroidism is the commonest manifestation and carries the highest parathyroid carcinoma risk of the hereditary hyperparathyroidism syndromes.
Ossifying fibromas of the mandible and maxilla are characteristic and are distinct from brown tumours, persisting even after the hyperparathyroidism is cured.
Parathyroid adenomas are frequently cystic, and carcinoma should be actively considered at diagnosis and at surgery.
Renal lesions (cysts, hamartomas, Wilms tumour, adult polycystic disease) and uterine tumours causing menorrhagia and subfertility occur.
Loss of nuclear parafibromin staining on immunohistochemistry supports a CDC73-related tumour.
Given the carcinoma risk, en bloc resection may be preferred over simple enucleation of an involved gland.
Lifelong surveillance for recurrent hyperparathyroidism and for jaw, renal and uterine tumours is needed, alongside cascade testing of relatives.
reference.pathophysiology: The hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumour syndrome is an autosomal dominant tumour-predisposition disorder caused by germline inactivating variants in CDC73 (formerly HRPT2), which encodes parafibromin, a component of the PAF1 transcriptional regulatory complex with tumour-suppressor activity. A somatic second hit within parathyroid tissue produces biallelic inactivation and neoplasia, giving primary hyperparathyroidism from parathyroid adenomas, which are characteristically cystic, or from carcinoma. Among the hereditary hyperparathyroidism syndromes this condition carries the greatest risk of parathyroid carcinoma. Loss of parafibromin also predisposes to ossifying (cemento-ossifying) fibromas of the mandible and maxilla, to renal lesions including cysts, hamartomas, Wilms tumour and adult polycystic disease, and to uterine tumours such as leiomyomas and adenofibromas. Loss of nuclear parafibromin staining on immunohistochemistry supports the diagnosis of a CDC73-related tumour.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 and type 2A
Familial isolated hyperparathyroidism (which may be allelic)
Brown tumours of hyperparathyroidism, as opposed to true ossifying fibroma
additionalInvestigations: Corrected serum calcium, parathyroid hormone and phosphate with urinary calcium
Neck ultrasound with sestamibi scintigraphy or four-dimensional CT for localisation
Panoramic jaw radiograph (orthopantomogram) or maxillofacial CT for ossifying fibromas
Renal ultrasound or CT for cysts, hamartoma or Wilms tumour
Pelvic ultrasound in women for uterine tumours
Parafibromin immunohistochemistry on resected tumour tissue
redFlags: Markedly elevated calcium and parathyroid hormone with a firm or fixed neck mass, suggesting parathyroid carcinoma
Local invasion or lymphadenopathy identified at operation
Haematuria or a renal mass suggesting Wilms tumour or hamartoma
Severe menorrhagia with anaemia from uterine tumours
reference.prognosis: Outlook depends largely on whether parathyroid carcinoma develops: benign disease managed with careful surgery and surveillance carries a good prognosis, whereas carcinoma may recur and metastasise and carries a worse prognosis.
pitfalls: Enucleating a parathyroid tumour without considering carcinoma, risking incomplete resection and recurrence
Mistaking an ossifying fibroma for a brown tumour and mismanaging the jaw lesion
Failing to test CDC73 in apparently sporadic parathyroid carcinoma
Omitting renal and uterine screening and cascade family testing
Assuming cure after parathyroidectomy and abandoning long-term follow-up
references: Clinical genetics references on hereditary endocrine tumour syndromes
Consensus guidelines on parathyroid carcinoma and hereditary hyperparathyroidism
management: Definitive surgical parathyroidectomy with en bloc resection of suspicious glands given the high risk of parathyroid carcinoma
Preoperative localisation and control of hypercalcaemia with hydration, bisphosphonates and a calcimimetic such as cinacalcet, particularly in unresectable or metastatic carcinoma
Maxillofacial surgical excision of symptomatic ossifying fibromas of the mandible and maxilla
Lifelong biochemical surveillance with corrected calcium and parathyroid hormone for recurrent or metastatic parathyroid carcinoma
Periodic imaging surveillance for renal lesions including cysts, hamartoma and Wilms tumour, with pelvic assessment for uterine tumours in women
Germline CDC73 testing with genetic counselling and cascade screening of relatives for autosomal dominant inheritance
Multidisciplinary management involving endocrine surgery, endocrinology, oncology and clinical genetics
